purpose: How a working gold-plating bench decides whether a customer's piece may be accepted at all and then converts that decision into evidence and informed consent before anything irreversible happens: identifying and photographing the piece, separating what the client reports from what the bench can actually verify, triaging irreplaceable and high-risk items against written refusal criteria, disclosing in writing what a plated finish is and is not (never solid gold, never a guaranteed wear life), gating every irreversible step behind a fresh approval, and closing the job with a before-and-after record that makes any later dispute decidable on evidence rather than memory.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

the shop plates with purchased commercial chemistry used per its supplier technical data sheet; intake never promises a bath setpoint, a thickness figure or a wear life as a fact, only the mechanism and how it will be verified
a customer piece is an object of unknown history until the bench verifies it; everything the client reports about metal, prior repairs or prior plating is a claim to be tested, not a measurement
the shop's own intake forms, liability wording and insurance arrangements are reviewed by its own counsel and insurer; nothing in this knowledge base is legal, financial or medical advice

regulated marking terms, nickel-release rules, secondhand-goods identification duties and personal-data retention rules differ by jurisdiction and must be verified locally before an intake form is used
exclusions: the price mechanism, service-menu design, minimum charges, batching and quote-validity windows against gold-price movement — that is the sibling service-design and job-pricing knowledge base; intake states scope and risk, not the number

jeweller, retailer and repair-shop trade accounts, replate-cycle repeat demand, courier and insurance handling of trade parcels, account ledgers and referral loops — that is the sibling trade-account knowledge base; this one covers the walk-in and consumer-piece counter

bench procedure itself: surface preparation, bath selection and health, rack and fixture design, current and time control, and the measurement methods used to verify thickness, adhesion, porosity or colour — those belong to the preparation, chemistry, execution and finish-quality specialists

determining what a marking or advertising term legally requires in a given market: gold plated, vermeil, gold filled and rolled gold are obligation classes owned by the safety and compliance specialist, and this knowledge base only enforces the counter-level rule that plated work is never represented or implied to be solid gold

appraisal: no valuation of a piece is offered as a professional opinion, and clients seeking a value are routed to a qualified appraiser; intake records only a declared value used to agree handling and liability class

medical guidance on metal sensitivity or chemical exposure; nickel-release and skin-reaction questions are routed to the regulation classes and to a clinician, never answered as a safety assurance at the counter
drafting contracts, waivers or insurance policies, and any jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion about liability limits

competency_questions.question: What must be true before a customer's piece is accepted across the counter at all, and who is allowed to accept it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INTAKE_MANDATE names the artifacts intake must produce and the accountable accept-or-refuse decision, and CUSTODY_AND_TAGGING states how physical custody is taken and proven

competency_questions.question: How is the piece documented at intake so that its condition on the day it arrived can be proved months later?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PIECE_DESCRIPTION_RECORD defines the written identification fields and CONDITION_PHOTO_PROTOCOL defines the dated photo set including macro shots of every existing flaw

competency_questions.question: What do I ask the client about the piece's history, and how much of their answer am I allowed to rely on?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CLIENT_HISTORY_INTERVIEW lists the questions that change bench decisions and SUBSTRATE_UNCERTAINTY_HANDLING states the rule that a client claim is recorded as a claim and an unknown is recorded as unknown

competency_questions.question: Which features on a piece raise process risk at the counter, and what does each one imply for whether and how the job can run?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RISK_FEATURE_SURVEY enumerates the feature classes (set stones, glued parts, hollow and capillary traps, enamel, springs and mechanisms, prior solder, worn-through zones) and gives each a handling decision or a stop

competency_questions.question: How is an irreplaceable piece handled differently from a replaceable one, and what does the value written on the ticket actually mean?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HEIRLOOM_RISK_TRIAGE separates sentimental irreplaceability from monetary value and routes the irreplaceable class to a higher refusal bar, and VALUATION_AND_LIABILITY_BASIS defines declared value and the shop's stated liability class without offering an appraisal

competency_questions.question: Which jobs does this shop refuse, and how is a refusal delivered so the client leaves respected rather than insulted?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: REFUSAL_CRITERIA states the written decline list and its precedence over revenue, and REFUSAL_DELIVERY gives the reason-alternative-referral structure and the recorded refusal note

competency_questions.question: How do I satisfy myself that the person handing me the piece is entitled to hand it over?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OWNERSHIP_AND_PROVENANCE_CHECK states the ownership question, the third-party and estate cases, the red flags that stop an intake, and the verify-your-jurisdiction identification duty

competency_questions.question: What exactly are we agreeing that the shop will do, and what are we agreeing it will not do?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SCOPE_OF_WORK_STATEMENT produces a written in-scope and out-of-scope statement naming the surfaces covered, the defects that will remain, and the components that will not be touched

competency_questions.question: How do I describe durability honestly to a client who wants to hear that it will last forever and look like solid gold?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: WEAR_EXPECTATION_DISCLOSURE explains coating life as a mechanism with no time guarantee, and NOT_SOLID_GOLD_REPRESENTATION states the absolute rule that plated work is never represented or implied to be solid gold and routes marking terms to the compliance classes

competency_questions.question: What has to be said out loud and in writing about existing damage and about colour before the piece goes anywhere near a strip tank or a polishing wheel?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PREEXISTING_DAMAGE_DISCLOSURE states that plating does not fill defects and that stripping and polishing remove metal and can open worn zones, and COLOR_MATCH_EXPECTATION bounds what a colour match can promise against a retained reference and a named viewing light

competency_questions.question: What completion date do I promise on a customer piece, and how do I handle the day it slips?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TURNAROUND_PROMISE builds the date from the named uncertain segments (queue, outside setter, cure and inspection hold, possible rework) and requires the client to be told of a slip as soon as the shop knows, not on the promised day

competency_questions.question: What does the client sign, and which bench steps require a fresh approval rather than relying on that signature?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RISK_ACKNOWLEDGMENT_SIGNOFF lists what the signed sheet must contain, IRREVERSIBLE_STEP_GATE names the steps that need per-step approval, and MIDJOB_DISCOVERY_ESCALATION defines the stop-and-call when the bench finds something intake missed

competency_questions.question: How is the finished piece handed back so a dispute cannot turn into one person's word against another's, and what happens when a complaint arrives anyway?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HANDOVER_ACCEPTANCE_RECORD pairs the before and after evidence with a client inspection and acceptance, AFTERCARE_INSTRUCTIONS supplies the written care mechanism, and COMPLAINT_AND_REDO_PROTOCOL decides defect versus expected wear from the retained record

glossary.definition: The single job record opened when a piece is accepted: tag number, client and contact, written description, condition photo set, history answers, risk features, declared value, agreed scope, disclosures given and the signature that authorises work to begin.

The dated before-images captured at the counter with the job tag in frame: every face of the piece plus a macro of each existing flaw (worn-through zone, pit, scratch, loose stone, prior repair), stored against the ticket so the piece's arrival state is provable later.

An intake classification for pieces whose loss or alteration cannot be made good by money or by remaking — a deceased parent's wedding band, a piece with a memorial engraving, an antique with original finish — which raises the refusal bar and forces per-step approval regardless of the declared value.

The value the client states for the piece at intake, recorded as the client's own figure and used only to agree handling, storage and liability class; it is never an appraisal by the shop and never presented as one.

The client-signed sheet that records the agreed scope, the disclosed risks of strip, polish, heat and chemistry on a used piece, the wear expectation for a plated finish, the irreplaceability class and the stated liability basis, referencing the condition photos by ticket number.

Any bench action that cannot be undone on this piece: stripping the existing plate, polishing or abrasive finishing, unsetting a stone, applying heat or solder, and any chemical immersion that can attack the substrate, a glued joint or a porous stone.

The standing rule that when the bench discovers something intake did not know — hidden soft solder, base metal under a worn plate, a cracked shank, a stone loose in its setting — work halts, the state is photographed and the client is contacted before another step is taken.

The physical sample or dated photograph of the target colour agreed at intake, viewed under a named light, against which the finished piece will be compared; a shop panel kept for this purpose plays the same role a master panel plays in batch colour checks at the bench.

An area where the previous plating has already worn to the base metal — ring shank undersides, bracelet link contact faces, clasp thumbpieces — which both predicts where the new deposit will wear first and warns that stripping and polishing may thin or open the substrate there.

The closing event of a customer job: the client inspects the finished piece against the agreed scope with the before and after images side by side, receives the care sheet and the restated wear expectation, and signs acceptance, after which the whole record is retained as the shop's evidence.

nodes.definition: Fix what intake is for before designing a single form: it is the shop's evidence-and-consent gate, the one moment when the piece, the client and the shop are in the same room and nothing irreversible has happened yet. Intake must leave behind four things a plating bench can never manufacture afterwards — a dated record of the piece's condition, a written statement of what will and will not be done, the client's informed agreement to the risks that strip, polish, heat and chemistry carry on a used object of unknown history, and a custody trail that proves which piece is which through the queue. It also fixes accountability: one named person decides accept or refuse on each job, and no piece enters the queue on a verbal 'we can probably do that'. A shop that treats intake as a receipt will process work it should have declined and will have nothing to show when a worn shank opens in the strip tank; a shop that treats intake as a gate accepts fewer jobs and loses almost none of them to dispute. What the job costs is decided next door in the service and pricing knowledge base; intake decides whether the job is allowed to exist.

included: the mandatory outputs of intake
who may accept a piece and who decides accept or refuse
the rule that no bench step precedes the record
excluded: quoting and the price mechanism
bench process choice
trade-account terms and courier logistics

pros.claim: Naming intake's required outputs turns a counter conversation into four artifacts that decide every later argument
pros.example: when a client returns claiming the shop cracked an enamel panel, the ticket's macro photo of that same crack ends the argument in a minute

pros.claim: A single accountable acceptor stops risky pieces from entering the queue through whoever happened to be free
pros.example: a Saturday helper who cannot judge a soldered antique brooch takes the details and books the owner back rather than accepting the job

cons.claim: A real gate adds minutes at the counter and costs some impulse walk-in work
cons.example: a client on a lunch break leaves rather than wait while photographs and a signature are completed

cons.claim: Intake discipline is invisible until it pays, so it is the first thing dropped in a busy week
cons.example: a pre-holiday rush where three chains are taken in on sticky notes and one comes back unidentifiable

failure_modes: treating intake as a receipt for a customer rather than a gate for the shop
starting bench work while the paperwork 'catches up' later in the day
letting the accept decision drift to whoever is at the counter when a hard piece arrives
acceptance_tests: the written intake policy names the four required outputs (condition record, scope statement, signed risk acknowledgment, custody tag) and the one person accountable for accept or refuse on each job
no job in the current queue can be found whose bench work started before its intake record was complete
revisit_triggers: a dispute or a loss is suffered because an intake artifact was missing
the shop adds a service class with a different risk profile, such as work with stones left in place
counter staffing changes so that people who did not write the policy are accepting pieces

base.update_signal: a job is lost, damaged or disputed and the post-mortem names a missing intake artifact or an unclear accept decision

nodes.definition: Take and prove physical custody the moment the piece leaves the client's hand: one piece to one numbered tag, that number written on the client's receipt and on the ticket, and the piece stored in its own labelled container rather than loose in a tray. The plating queue is unusually hostile to identity — pieces are stripped of the finish that made them recognisable, they travel between counter, polishing motor, prep bench, tanks and rinse, and several identical-looking chains from different clients can be in the shop on the same afternoon. The custody rule is therefore that the tag never leaves the piece unless it physically cannot enter a bath, in which case the piece moves in a numbered, single-job carrier and the tag travels with the carrier, and every transfer between stations is logged so an unaccounted-for piece is discovered in minutes rather than at closing. Small parts that can vanish down a sink or a drain — earring backs, stone-set head assemblies, split rings — are counted at intake and counted again at handover, with the count written on the ticket.

included: one-piece-one-tag numbering
single-job containers and station-to-station logging
small-part counts at intake and handover
excluded: courier and insured shipping of trade parcels
rack and fixture design at the bench
shop insurance policy selection

pros.claim: A tag that never leaves the piece survives the moment plating destroys visual identification
pros.example: two thin curb chains stripped on the same morning stay distinguishable only because each sat in its own numbered carrier

pros.claim: Counting small parts at intake converts a devastating loss into a boring reconciliation
pros.example: four earring backs counted in and four counted out means the client's missing back was never in the shop

cons.claim: Single-job carriers and per-station logging cost time and space and resist batching efficiency
cons.example: a run that could have gone into one basket instead needs separate carriers because the pieces belong to different clients

cons.claim: Tags themselves interact with the process and must be chosen for it
cons.example: a paper tag left on a piece into a hot cleaning stage disintegrates and leaves the piece anonymous in the rinse

failure_modes: batching several clients' pieces into one basket because they look similar and are 'obviously' distinguishable
removing the tag for a photograph or a polish and putting the piece down untagged
no small-part count, so a missing earring back becomes an unwinnable argument
acceptance_tests: every piece currently in the shop can be traced to a ticket number by its tag or its numbered carrier without relying on anyone's memory
the ticket for each job records the piece count and small-part count taken at intake
revisit_triggers: any piece is temporarily unlocatable during a working day
a new process stage is added that a tag cannot travel through
job volume rises to the point where multiple similar pieces routinely coexist in the queue

base.update_signal: a custody incident (misidentified, mislaid or lost piece) or a change in process stages that the current tagging scheme cannot survive

nodes.definition: Write down what the piece is in terms specific enough that a stranger could pick it out of a tray and a court could tell it from a substitute: item class and form, approximate dimensions, mass on the shop balance, the number and type of stones with any that are loose or chipped called out, the construction features that matter to plating (hollow or solid, hinged, spring-loaded, glued components, enamel or resin, mixed metal colours), and any marks read from the piece. Marks are recorded as marks, not as facts: a stamp reading a fineness or a maker's name is what the piece says about itself, and on a piece that has already been plated once it may be describing the core, the previous coating or nothing at all. The record exists to do three jobs — to prevent substitution disputes, to give the bench the information it needs before the piece reaches it, and to give the counter a written basis for the risk conversation that follows. Anything the counter cannot determine is written as unknown rather than guessed.

included: identification fields that distinguish this piece from a similar one
marks recorded as claims the piece makes
stone count and condition noted as observed
excluded: appraised or market value
gemstone identification as a professional opinion
metal assay conclusions

pros.claim: A description precise enough to defeat substitution protects both the client and the shop
pros.example: recording 'nine-link bracelet, one link with an old solder patch on the underside' identifies that exact bracelet later

pros.claim: Weighing the piece at intake creates a cheap, checkable constant across the job
pros.example: a mass re-checked at handover shows nothing was swapped and how little metal polishing actually removed

cons.claim: Written descriptions can be read as expert assertions the shop never intended to make
cons.example: writing 'gold ring' rather than 'yellow-coloured ring, stamped mark noted' invites a later claim that the shop confirmed the metal

cons.claim: Thorough description takes counter time that scales badly with multi-piece intakes
cons.example: an estate lot of a dozen small items turns a five-minute counter visit into a booked-in appointment

failure_modes: recording a stamped mark as a verified metal fact
describing pieces so generically that two clients' items read identically on the tickets
omitting the stone count, so a chipped or missing stone has no baseline
acceptance_tests: each ticket's description distinguishes its piece from every other piece in the shop that week without the tag
every mark on the ticket is phrased as a mark observed on the piece rather than as a metal or fineness conclusion
stone count and any pre-existing stone damage are recorded before the piece leaves the counter
revisit_triggers: a client questions whether the returned piece is the one they left
a new item class enters the service mix whose description needs different fields, such as watch cases or eyewear
the bench reports that ticket descriptions do not tell it what it needs before starting

base.update_signal: a substitution or identification dispute, or bench feedback that the description field set omits something it needs

nodes.definition: Photograph the piece at the counter, before any cleaning, handling or bench work, to a fixed routine: all faces of the item, the tag in frame or the tag number visible in the same shot, a scale reference, and a close macro of every existing defect — worn-through zones where old plating has gone to base metal, pits and porosity, scratches and dents, chipped stones, loose settings, prior repairs and solder patches, engraving and hallmarks that polishing could soften. Lighting and background are kept consistent so the after images are comparable rather than merely prettier, and the file set is attached to the ticket the same day with its capture date intact. The reason is mechanical, not bureaucratic: plating processes reveal and amplify what was already there, a polished or stripped surface no longer carries the evidence of its former state, and the single most common consumer dispute in this trade is about a flaw the client first noticed after collection. The rule that makes the protocol work is that the flaw the counter is tempted to skip photographing is exactly the flaw that will be argued about.

included: the before image set and its capture routine
macro documentation of every pre-existing defect
consistent lighting and dating so before and after are comparable
excluded: laboratory imaging or measurement for quality release
microscope defect diagnosis at the bench
marketing photography of finished work

pros.claim: Dated macro evidence converts the commonest dispute class from opinion into comparison
pros.example: the client who says the shop dented the bezel is shown the same dent, dated, with their own tag in frame

pros.claim: The photo pass forces a slow visual inspection that catches risk features the eye skips in conversation
pros.example: photographing the underside of a shank is often the moment a hairline crack is first seen

cons.claim: Images are only as useful as their consistency, and casual capture produces unusable comparisons
cons.example: a warm-lit before shot against a cool-lit after shot makes an unchanged colour look like a colour failure

cons.claim: Storing client images creates a personal-data retention duty the shop must handle deliberately
cons.example: photo sets accumulating on a personal phone with no retention or access rule, in a jurisdiction whose privacy rules must be checked

failure_modes: photographing after a quick clean, destroying the arrival-state evidence
wide shots only, so no macro exists of the defect that later matters
images that cannot be tied to a ticket because the tag was out of frame
acceptance_tests: every accepted job has a dated before set covering all faces plus one macro per recorded defect, tied to its ticket number
before and after images for a completed job are visually comparable in framing and lighting
revisit_triggers: a dispute turns on a defect that the before set does not show
the shop changes camera, lighting or storage location for job images
privacy or retention rules applicable in the shop's jurisdiction change

base.update_signal: a dispute the image set could not settle, or a change in imaging equipment, storage or retention obligations

nodes.definition: Ask the small set of questions whose answers actually change what the bench may do, and ask them in the order that keeps the client comfortable: has the piece been plated or refinished before and roughly when, has it ever been repaired, resized or soldered, is anything on it glued rather than set, is it worn daily and on which hand, has it been in contact with pools, cleaners, perfumes or hand sanitiser, has the client ever reacted to it against the skin, and what would count as success for them today. Each answer routes somewhere concrete: a prior repair warns of soft solder and heat sensitivity; glue warns that solvents and hot cleaning stages may release a component; daily wear tells the bench where the finish will be attacked first; a reported skin reaction is routed to the nickel-release regulation class and to the client's own clinician rather than answered as a safety assurance at the counter; and the client's definition of success is what the scope statement will have to satisfy or correct. Answers are recorded verbatim as the client's account, with 'client does not know' as a completely acceptable and frequently correct entry.

included: the question set whose answers change bench decisions
recording answers as the client's account
routing a reported skin reaction to regulation classes and professional care
excluded: any medical opinion on sensitivity or allergy
verifying the answers, which happens at the bench
credit or account terms, which belong to the trade-account knowledge base

pros.claim: A short fixed question set surfaces the hazards that intake inspection alone cannot see
pros.example: the client mentioning a repair after a break years ago is the only warning that soft solder may sit under the old plating

pros.claim: Asking what success looks like exposes an impossible expectation while it is still free to correct
pros.example: a client who says they want it to look like the day it was bought is really asking for material removal that would soften an engraving

cons.claim: Client memory is unreliable and sometimes flatly wrong, so answers can mislead if trusted as fact
cons.example: a piece confidently described as never repaired that shows an obvious solder seam under magnification

cons.claim: An interview that feels like an interrogation costs goodwill on a small job
cons.example: eleven questions asked about a simple chain refresh when three would have changed anything

failure_modes: recording client claims as verified facts on the ticket
skipping the prior-repair question, which is the single most useful one for heat and chemistry risk
answering a skin-reaction question with a reassurance instead of a referral
acceptance_tests: every ticket carries answers to the prior-plating, prior-repair, glued-component, wear-pattern and skin-reaction questions, with unknown recorded where it is the truth
no ticket contains a skin-safety assurance given at the counter
revisit_triggers: the bench repeatedly finds conditions the interview should have surfaced
a new service class is offered whose risks depend on different history
regulatory guidance on skin-contact metals in the shop's market changes

base.update_signal: bench discoveries that a history question would have predicted, or a change in the service mix that makes different history relevant

nodes.definition: Decide and record, item by item, what is genuinely known about the piece and what is merely believed, because almost every intake mistake in this trade is an unknown promoted to a fact. At the counter the shop can observe form, marks, magnetism, colour and obvious construction; it cannot see through an existing coating to the core, cannot tell an old soft-solder repair from a hard one without magnification and sometimes not even then, and cannot read a base metal through a plated skin with a surface technique whose reading depth is comparable to the coating itself — the same limitation that makes a fineness reading taken through a thin gold layer untrustworthy in a quality lab. Destructive or marking tests are not run on a client's piece at intake without explicit permission, and the honest counter position is therefore a written unknowns list with a verification plan: what will be checked at the bench before the irreversible step, what will be checked by the supplier's data or a laboratory if a claim must be made, and what will simply be treated as risk the client accepts. The rule is that an unknown never silently becomes an assumption in the scope statement, the timeline or the risk sheet.

included: separating observed from believed at the counter
the unknowns list and its verification plan
the rule that no destructive or marking test runs on a client piece without permission
excluded: the measurement methods themselves, which belong to the finish-quality specialist
assay and laboratory certification procedures
buying decisions about instruments

pros.claim: An explicit unknowns list keeps the scope statement honest and gives the bench a checklist before the irreversible step
pros.example: 'core metal unknown beneath existing plate, confirm at prep before strip' written on the ticket rather than assumed to be brass

pros.claim: Naming uncertainty out loud at the counter is itself an expectation-setting act the client remembers
pros.example: telling a client that what lies under a worn coating cannot be seen until it is off, so the outcome may change

cons.claim: Clients read honest uncertainty as incompetence unless it comes with a plan
cons.example: a client comparing the shop unfavourably with a competitor who confidently promised a result on the same unknown piece

cons.claim: Verification steps consume bench time and sometimes gold before any billable work begins
cons.example: a test area worked on an inconspicuous surface only to establish what the substrate is

failure_modes: guessing the core metal from a stamped mark and building the whole plan on it
running a marking or destructive test on a client's piece without asking first
leaving the unknowns list off the ticket so the bench inherits assumptions rather than questions
acceptance_tests: each ticket separates observed facts from client claims and from unknowns, and every unknown has either a verification step or an explicit accepted-risk note
no client piece has been subjected to a marking or destructive test without a recorded permission
revisit_triggers: an unknown that was treated as accepted risk causes a loss or a dispute
the shop gains or loses access to a verification method
recurring bench surprises show the counter is systematically over-confident about a piece class

base.update_signal: a bench finding that contradicts an intake assumption, or a change in what the shop can verify before the irreversible step

nodes.definition: Walk the piece under a loupe against a fixed feature list, because the plating queue punishes specific physical features rather than pieces in general. The classes that matter: stones set in place, since heat-sensitive and porous material such as pearl, opal, turquoise, emerald and any treated or fracture-filled stone can be damaged by cleaning chemistry, ultrasonics and elevated-temperature baths; glued components and adhesive-set stones, which solvents and hot stages can release; hollow forms, tubes, lockets and rolled edges that trap solution and bleed it out later as staining or corrosion; enamel, resin, patina and intentionally oxidised finishes that a strip or a polish destroys; springs, hinges, clasps and mechanisms whose function must survive the process; prior repairs and soft solder that behave differently in heat and chemistry; mixed metals and part-plated assemblies that will not finish uniformly; and worn-through zones where the substrate is already thin. Each flagged feature ends in one of three recorded outcomes — handled by a named method, excluded from scope, or a stop that sends the job to the refusal criteria — and none of them may be left as an open question on an accepted job.

included: the feature classes that change or stop a plating job
the handle, exclude or stop decision per flagged feature
the loupe inspection that finds them at the counter
excluded: the bench method chosen to handle a feature, which belongs to the preparation and execution specialists
gemstone identification as a professional opinion
bath chemistry selection

pros.claim: A fixed feature list catches the hazards that experience alone forgets under counter pressure
pros.example: a locket photographed and accepted without anyone asking whether solution trapped in the hollow can escape

pros.claim: Forcing every flag to a handle, exclude or stop decision means no risk enters the queue undecided
pros.example: a glued-in cabochon recorded as excluded from immersion, with that exclusion written into the scope statement

cons.claim: Loupe survey at the counter is slow and still misses what sits under the existing coating
cons.example: a soft-solder seam invisible until the old plate comes off, which no counter inspection would have found

cons.claim: An over-cautious survey turns routine work into an escalation queue
cons.example: flagging every set stone as a stop when many stable stones tolerate the shop's normal process

failure_modes: no loupe pass at all, so glue lines and hairline cracks are found only at the bench
flagging a feature without recording a decision, leaving the bench to improvise
treating an unfamiliar stone as safe because it looks like a familiar one
acceptance_tests: each ticket shows the feature list worked through, with every flagged feature carrying a handled, excluded or stopped decision
no accepted job contains a flagged feature whose handling is left to bench judgement without a record
revisit_triggers: a feature class not on the list causes damage or a mid-job stop
the shop changes a process stage in a way that alters which features are dangerous
a new material or stone type starts appearing regularly in intake

base.update_signal: damage or a mid-job stop traced to a feature the survey does not cover, or a process change that alters feature risk

nodes.definition: Classify every incoming piece on a second axis that has nothing to do with money: whether a loss or an irreversible alteration could be made good at all. A modest chain with a high declared value is replaceable; a worn wedding band from a deceased spouse, a christening bracelet, an antique with its original finish and hand engraving, or a piece carrying a memorial inscription is not, at any price. The question is asked directly and gently at the counter — whether this piece could be replaced if the worst happened — and the answer is recorded as a class on the ticket, because that class, not the value, is what changes the shop's behaviour: irreplaceable pieces get the higher refusal bar, per-step approval rather than blanket authorisation, the most conservative process option even where a more aggressive one would look better, and a written acknowledgment that the shop's liability can compensate a loss but can never replace the object. This is also the class where the honest answer is most often to decline, and the specialist's standing rule is that no single job is worth an irreplaceable loss.

included: the replaceable versus irreplaceable classification and how it is asked
the behaviour changes the irreplaceable class triggers
the honest statement that money cannot restore such a piece
excluded: monetary appraisal
insurance product selection
the price consequences of extra care, which belong to the pricing knowledge base

pros.claim: Separating irreplaceability from value stops a cheap heirloom from being treated as a low-stakes job
pros.example: a thin worn band of little metal value handled with the same care as the highest-value item on the bench

pros.claim: Asking the question early gives the client a real chance to choose not to risk the piece
pros.example: a client deciding to leave a grandmother's ring untouched and to plate a modern piece instead

cons.claim: The conversation is emotionally heavy and can turn a routine intake into a difficult moment
cons.example: a recently bereaved client asked directly whether the ring could be replaced

cons.claim: The class raises handling cost on jobs whose ticket value cannot support it
cons.example: a small memorial locket demanding per-step approvals and the slowest process the shop has

failure_modes: inferring irreplaceability from value instead of asking
recording the class but not changing any behaviour because of it
accepting an irreplaceable piece with a high process risk because the client insisted
acceptance_tests: every ticket carries a replaceable or irreplaceable class recorded from the client's own answer
every ticket in the irreplaceable class shows the elevated handling it triggered: per-step approval and the conservative process option
revisit_triggers: an irreplaceable piece is damaged, lost or altered beyond restoration
the shop finds itself routinely accepting irreplaceable pieces with unresolved risk features
a service class is added that is inherently unsuitable for irreplaceable items

base.update_signal: an incident involving an irreplaceable piece, or evidence that the class is being recorded without changing handling

nodes.definition: Settle before work starts what value is being used for this job and what the shop's exposure is if something goes wrong, without ever slipping into appraisal. The value on the ticket is the client's declared figure, written as their statement; the shop does not confirm it, does not offer a market opinion, and refers clients who need a valuation to a qualified appraiser. The declared value then drives mechanism, not sentiment: which storage and custody class the piece goes into, whether it is inside or outside the shop's insurance arrangements, whether extra handling or a witness is required, and what the shop's written liability position is on the risk acknowledgment. That position is stated in plain language and reviewed by the shop's own insurer and counsel, because liability wording is jurisdiction-specific and this is a commercial mechanism rather than legal advice. Where the piece is also in the irreplaceable class, the sheet says plainly that a liability figure compensates a loss but does not restore the object, so the real protection is the refusal criteria and the approval gates, not the number.

included: declared value recorded as the client's own statement
the handling, storage and insurance class the declared value selects
plain-language liability position on the risk sheet
excluded: appraisal or market valuation by the shop
selecting or interpreting an insurance policy
any jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion about enforceability

pros.claim: A declared value recorded as the client's own statement sets handling class without the shop ever appraising
pros.example: a piece the client declares above the shop's ordinary handling threshold going straight into the secure-storage and witness routine

pros.claim: Stating the liability position before work removes the worst surprise from any later incident
pros.example: the client learning what the shop does and does not cover on the day they hand the piece over rather than the day it is damaged

cons.claim: Talking about liability at intake dampens the mood and can read as expecting failure
cons.example: a client asking why the shop is discussing loss before it has even looked at the job

cons.claim: Declared values are unverified and can be inflated, distorting handling and any later claim
cons.example: a costume piece declared at a value its metal and stones could not support

failure_modes: letting a declared value be read as the shop's valuation
using a liability cap as a substitute for refusing an unsuitable job
wording written from a template without the shop's own insurer and counsel reviewing it
acceptance_tests: the ticket shows the value as the client's declaration and contains no shop valuation statement
the liability wording used on customer jobs is the version reviewed by the shop's own insurer and counsel, and the review date is recorded
revisit_triggers: the shop's insurance arrangements or their conditions change
a claim or near-claim exposes wording that did not do what the shop assumed
the service mix starts including declared values above the current handling classes

base.update_signal: a change in the shop's insurance arrangements, or a claim that shows the stated liability basis behaved differently than assumed

nodes.definition: Establish that the person across the counter is entitled to authorise irreversible work on the piece, because a plating job permanently changes an object that may belong to somebody else. The routine is light for ordinary work and firmer as value, irreplaceability and irreversibility rise: ask whose piece it is, record the owner separately from the person delivering it when they differ, obtain the owner's authorisation directly for anything irreversible, and treat estate and probate pieces as needing the executor or the family's agreed representative rather than whichever relative arrives first. Red flags are handled as a stop rather than an accusation — a bag of assorted pieces with no history, urgency to have identifying marks polished away, an unwillingness to give any contact details, or a request to remove or obscure an engraving or hallmark. Identification duties for secondhand or high-value goods vary by jurisdiction and must be verified locally; the intake rule the shop can always keep is that unresolved entitlement stops the job before any irreversible step and the piece is returned unworked.

included: recording owner separately from the person delivering
authorisation for irreversible work from the owner
red flags that stop an intake and the verify-your-jurisdiction identification duty
excluded: any legal determination of title
acting as an authority or making accusations
trade-account and courier deliveries, which the trade-account knowledge base handles

pros.claim: Separating owner from bearer prevents the shop from acting on an authorisation that was never the owner's
pros.example: a partner dropping off a ring for resizing and replating who cannot authorise polishing away an inscription

pros.claim: A stop-not-accuse rule lets the counter decline safely without a confrontation
pros.example: declining a lot of unidentified pieces politely on the shop's stated policy rather than challenging the person

cons.claim: Entitlement questions can offend legitimate clients if applied heavily to routine work
cons.example: asking for identification on a small chain refresh from a regular customer

cons.claim: The shop cannot actually verify title and can only document what it was told
cons.example: a plausible account of inheritance that the shop has no way to confirm either way

failure_modes: accepting irreversible work from a bearer without the owner's authorisation
treating a red flag as a customer-service problem to be smoothed over
applying an identification routine that the shop's jurisdiction does not permit or requires differently
acceptance_tests: on every job where the bearer is not the owner, the ticket records both and shows the owner's authorisation before any irreversible step
the shop's identification routine is documented against the rules verified for its own jurisdiction, with a check date
revisit_triggers: a piece is claimed by someone other than the client who left it
local secondhand-goods or identification rules change
the shop begins accepting estate lots or third-party drop-offs regularly

base.update_signal: an ownership dispute over a piece in the shop, or a change in local identification and secondhand-goods obligations

nodes.definition: Write down, before the difficult piece arrives, the jobs this shop does not take, so the decision is made by policy at rest rather than by a tired person in front of a hopeful client. The list is built from the intersection of consequence and uncertainty rather than from difficulty alone: an irreplaceable piece carrying an unresolved high-risk feature; a piece whose substrate cannot be verified before an irreversible step and whose owner will not accept that risk in writing; heat- or chemistry-sensitive set stones the client will not have unset; enamel, patina or original antique finish that the requested work would destroy; any job that can only succeed if the shop makes a representation it will not make, such as describing plated work as solid gold; any job the safety and compliance verdict blocks; and any job where entitlement is unresolved. Each entry names the trigger and the standard sentence used to decline it. The precedence rule is absolute: refusal criteria outrank revenue, a full diary, a regular client's goodwill and any signature the client is willing to give, because a waiver does not restore a destroyed heirloom.

included: the written decline list and its triggers
precedence of refusal over revenue and over client waivers
the requirement that each entry has a prepared decline sentence
excluded: declining work purely because it is unprofitable, which the pricing knowledge base owns
the compliance verdict itself, which belongs to the safety and compliance specialist
how the refusal is delivered, which is its own unit

pros.claim: A list written in calm conditions survives the moment a persuasive client is standing at the counter
pros.example: the counter reading out the shop's standing policy on unsettable heat-sensitive stones instead of improvising an exception

pros.claim: Explicit precedence over waivers prevents the false comfort that a signature makes a bad job acceptable
pros.example: declining a memorial ring with a cracked shank even though the client offers to sign anything

cons.claim: Every criterion turns away revenue the shop could sometimes have handled safely
cons.example: refusing a whole class of stone-set work that a shop with an unsetting bench partner could take

cons.claim: A rigid list ages badly as the shop's capability grows
cons.example: a criterion written before the shop had a reliable stripping and inspection routine still blocking work it could now do

failure_modes: keeping the criteria in someone's head instead of on paper
making an exception for a good customer and setting the precedent that the list is negotiable
using a signed waiver as the reason to take a job the list refuses
acceptance_tests: the decline list exists in writing with a trigger and a prepared sentence for each entry, dated and visible at the counter
every declined job in the record names the criterion that triggered it, and no accepted job matches a criterion
revisit_triggers: a job that met no criterion still ended in damage or dispute
the shop's capability changes so a criterion is now over-restrictive
the compliance specialist adds an obligation class that must become a decline trigger

base.update_signal: an incident on a job that met no criterion, or a capability or compliance change that adds or retires a trigger

nodes.definition: Deliver the refusal in a form that leaves the client with a usable path and the shop with a clean record, because how a shop says no is a large part of its reputation among jewellers and the public. The structure is short and repeatable: name the specific physical reason in plain language, say what the shop will not risk and why in one sentence, offer the alternative it can do if one exists, and refer onward when someone else genuinely should do the work. It never disparages the client, the piece or the shop that plated it last, never implies the client should have known better, and never leaves the impression that a different amount of money would have changed the answer, because that is precisely the invitation to press. The refusal is logged with its criterion, the date and what was offered instead, so the shop can see which criteria are costing it work and whether a capability investment would change the answer honestly. Where a piece is returned unworked after partial assessment, it goes back in its intake condition with its photo set intact.

included: the reason, alternative and referral structure of a decline
logging refusals with their criterion and offered alternative
returning an assessed piece in its intake condition
excluded: deciding what to refuse, which the criteria unit owns
referral fee or reciprocity arrangements, which belong to the trade-account knowledge base
price negotiation

pros.claim: A prepared decline script keeps refusals consistent and unemotional under pressure
pros.example: the same two sentences used for every unsettable heat-sensitive stone, whoever is at the counter

pros.claim: Offering a real alternative converts many refusals into smaller accepted jobs or future goodwill
pros.example: declining a full restore on an enamelled piece but offering to refresh only the plain band

cons.claim: Referring work onward can send a client to a competitor who takes the risky job anyway
cons.example: the client returning later with the piece damaged elsewhere and an expectation that this shop will fix it

cons.claim: A script delivered mechanically reads as indifference on an emotional piece
cons.example: a bereavement-linked item declined in the same flat wording used for a costume bracelet

failure_modes: explaining the refusal in terms the client hears as blame
softening the refusal into a maybe, which reopens the negotiation
not logging refusals, so the shop never learns what its criteria cost
acceptance_tests: each logged refusal records the criterion, the reason given, the alternative offered and the referral if any
a returned unworked piece leaves the shop in its documented intake condition with the photo set retained
revisit_triggers: refusal volume in one criterion rises enough to question the criterion or the capability behind it
clients report the refusal as rude or confusing
a referral partner stops being an appropriate onward route

base.update_signal: refusal-log patterns showing a criterion is costing disproportionate work, or client feedback that the decline landed badly

nodes.definition: Convert the assessment into one short written statement of what the shop will do to this piece and, at equal length, what it will not, because the yardstick used at handover has to exist before the work does. In scope names the surfaces and components covered, the service class agreed (a light decorative refresh, a heavier replate, or a strip-and-refinish restore, whose menu and price live in the service-design knowledge base), and the finishing that goes with it. Out of scope is written explicitly and is where disputes are actually prevented: the scratches that will remain because removing them would take metal the piece cannot spare, the stone that will not be unset, the interior that will not be reached, the worn engraving that will not be re-cut, the clasp that will be plated but not repaired, the second earring the client did not bring. Where a component is excluded from immersion or heat it is named. The statement is written in the client's own language rather than bench vocabulary, read back or handed over, and any change to it after work starts is treated as a new agreement rather than a bench decision.

included: what will be done, surface by surface and component by component
the explicit out-of-scope list including defects that will remain
the rule that scope changes only by a new agreement
excluded: the price and the quote-validity window, owned by the pricing knowledge base
the bench route chosen to achieve the scope
durability claims, which are their own disclosure

pros.claim: A written out-of-scope list is the single most effective dispute preventer in customer plating work
pros.example: the deep scratch on a bangle named as remaining, so its presence at handover surprises nobody

pros.claim: Writing scope in the client's language exposes misunderstandings while they are still cheap
pros.example: discovering at intake that the client meant the whole necklace, not just the pendant, before any work is booked

cons.claim: Detailed scope statements take counter time and can make a small job feel bureaucratic
cons.example: a two-line refresh job carrying a scope statement longer than the job description

cons.claim: An over-tight scope leaves the bench no room for a small improvement the client would have wanted
cons.example: a clasp that could have been eased in seconds left untouched because it was written out of scope

failure_modes: listing only what will be done and leaving exclusions to be assumed
using bench vocabulary the client agrees to without understanding
letting the bench quietly extend the scope because the piece 'needed it'
acceptance_tests: every accepted job carries a scope statement with a populated out-of-scope section naming the defects that will remain and the components not touched
any change to scope after work started is recorded as a new client agreement with its own approval
revisit_triggers: a handover dispute turns on something the scope statement did not address
the service menu changes so scope templates no longer match what is sold
the bench repeatedly needs to extend scope on a piece class

base.update_signal: a dispute or a scope extension that the current statement template did not anticipate

nodes.definition: Hold the line that a plated finish is a coating on another metal and is never represented, described, implied or allowed to be assumed as solid gold — not in speech at the counter, not on the ticket, not in the shop's advertising, and not by silence when a client says something untrue about what they are buying. Practically this means the shop states the service as plating on the client's existing piece, corrects a client who describes the outcome as making it gold, refuses to word a receipt or a card in a way that would help a piece be resold as solid, and declines the job outright if the client's purpose requires that misrepresentation. It also means the shop does not invent the regulated vocabulary: terms such as gold plated, vermeil, gold filled and rolled gold carry defined obligations that differ by market and attach to measurable properties, so any marking or descriptive claim goes to the safety and compliance specialist and the current rules for the shop's own jurisdiction are verified rather than remembered. Where the client wants a durable statement about what the finish is, the honest answer is what was applied over what, verified how — never a fineness claim read through a thin coating.

included: the counter-level rule and its wording
correcting a client's misdescription rather than letting it stand
routing marking and descriptive terms to the compliance obligation classes
excluded: deciding what a marking term legally requires in a given market
hallmarking submissions
laboratory verification methods and certificates

pros.claim: One absolute rule removes an entire class of judgement calls and the exposure that comes with them
pros.example: the counter answering a request to write gold on the receipt with the same refusal every time

pros.claim: Correcting the description early prevents a resale downstream that the shop unknowingly enabled
pros.example: a client planning to sell a plated piece online being told plainly what it is before the work is agreed

cons.claim: Insisting on accurate language deflates a client's excitement and occasionally loses the sale
cons.example: a client who wanted to hear that a piece would be gold now leaving to find a less careful shop

cons.claim: Regulated terminology is market-specific, so the shop must keep verifying rather than settling the wording once
cons.example: wording learned for one market being wrong for a client buying in another

failure_modes: letting a client's inaccurate description pass unchallenged because contradicting them is awkward
using a regulated term as a marketing flourish without checking what it obliges
issuing paperwork that a reseller could present as a fineness claim
acceptance_tests: no document the shop issues on plated work states or implies solid gold, and the counter has a standard correcting sentence in use
every regulated marking or descriptive term the shop uses is traced to a verified current rule for its own jurisdiction, with a check date
revisit_triggers: marking, advertising or consumer rules in the shop's market change
a client is found to have resold a plated piece using the shop's paperwork
the shop begins serving a new market with different terminology obligations

base.update_signal: a change in marking or consumer-protection rules in the shop's market, or a discovered misuse of shop paperwork in a resale

nodes.definition: Explain durability as a mechanism the client can reason about instead of a number the shop cannot honour. A plated layer is thin and finite, and how long it looks new depends on what the deposit is and how hard it is, how thick it is where the piece is actually rubbed, where the contact and abrasion zones sit on that particular item, and how the wearer lives — a ring on a working hand and a pendant worn occasionally are different problems on the same bench. The disclosure states plainly that a decorative refresh is cosmetic and will wear at contact points first, that a heavier deposit lasts longer for a proportionally higher gold and time cost, that no honest shop gives a wear time in months or years for a customer's used piece because the wearer's habits and the underlying substrate dominate, and that the shop's own verification is of what it applied, not of how long it will survive. Qualitative bands and the mechanism are given in writing on customer pieces; the client is told what would make it last longer and what would make it fail fast, and that the piece can be re-plated when it wears, which is the normal life cycle of plated jewellery rather than a failure.

included: the mechanism that governs how long a plated finish looks new
written qualitative disclosure with no time guarantee
framing re-plating as the normal cycle
excluded: thickness figures, bath setpoints and hardness numbers, which come from the process and finish specialists and the supplier data
wear-test methods and their acceptance criteria
warranty or refund terms, which sit in the complaint protocol

pros.claim: A mechanism explanation lets the client choose specification knowingly instead of hoping
pros.example: a client choosing the heavier option for a daily-worn ring once they understand where it will rub first

pros.claim: Refusing to name a lifespan removes the promise most likely to be quoted back at the shop
pros.example: never having said six months when a client with a workshop job wears through in six weeks

cons.claim: Clients want a number and can read its absence as evasion
cons.example: a client pressing for how long will it last and hearing an explanation instead of an answer

cons.claim: Honest wear disclosure suppresses some sales of the cheapest service class
cons.example: a client declining a light refresh once told it is cosmetic and will show wear at contact points first

failure_modes: offering a lifespan in months or years to close a hesitant sale
giving the disclosure verbally only, so at handover it is one person's word against another's
implying the shop's process verification is a durability guarantee
acceptance_tests: the written disclosure given on every customer piece states the wear mechanism and contains no time-based guarantee
the client's file shows which service class they chose after the disclosure, so specification and expectation are linked
revisit_triggers: complaints cluster on a service class, suggesting the disclosure is not landing
the shop changes deposit type or process so the honest description of durability changes
the finish-quality specialist reports wear behaviour that contradicts the current wording

base.update_signal: a cluster of wear complaints against one service class, or a process change that alters how durability must honestly be described

nodes.definition: Tell the client, before agreement, what the process will do to damage that is already on the piece, because plating is a mirror rather than a filler. A deposit follows the surface it is put on: pits, porosity, casting flaws, scratches, dents and pitted old solder stay visible and can look sharper under a bright new finish. Polishing does not remove damage for free — it removes metal, which softens engraving and hallmarks, rounds crisp edges and thins a shank that may already be worn. Stripping an old coating removes the material that was holding a thin worn zone together, and a shank or a link that is close to failure can open on the wheel, in the tank or in the ultrasonic rather than at some polite later date. The counter names the specific zones on this piece where each of these applies, points at them in the condition photos, and records the client's decision for each: accept as is, accept the metal loss that improving it requires, or leave it out of scope. The disclosure is written, not spoken, because it is the exact thing a disappointed client will later say they were never told.

included: how a deposit reproduces existing surface defects
metal loss from polishing and its effect on engraving and thin zones
the risk that stripping opens an already worn area, recorded per zone
excluded: the preparation and polishing technique itself
structural repair work such as re-shanking or re-tipping
defect diagnosis on finished work, which the finish-quality specialist owns

pros.claim: Naming defects zone by zone against the photos makes the disclosure concrete rather than boilerplate
pros.example: pointing at the thin underside of a shank in the macro shot and writing that it may open during strip

pros.claim: Recording accept-as-is decisions per defect converts later complaints into a reference to a signed choice
pros.example: the client who chose to keep the deep scratch rather than lose metal is shown their own recorded decision

cons.claim: A frank damage conversation can make a client feel their treasured piece is being criticised
cons.example: an inherited ring described defect by defect while its owner listens

cons.claim: Predicting which worn zone will open is genuinely uncertain, so the disclosure is a risk statement rather than a forecast
cons.example: a shank that survives strip perfectly after being flagged as likely to fail

failure_modes: generic wording about wear and tear instead of this piece's specific zones
promising that polishing will remove a defect without stating what it costs in metal
leaving the disclosure verbal on exactly the jobs most likely to be disputed
acceptance_tests: each recorded defect on the ticket carries a client decision of accept as is, improve at the stated metal cost, or out of scope
any zone identified as at risk of opening during strip or polish is named in writing and referenced to its condition photo
revisit_triggers: a piece fails at a zone the disclosure did not name
the shop changes stripping or polishing methods in a way that changes the risk
a defect class starts recurring in complaints

base.update_signal: a failure at an undisclosed zone, or a change in strip and polish method that shifts which zones are at risk

nodes.definition: Bound the colour conversation at intake, because matching is the expectation most often assumed and least often stated. Agree the target by pointing at something physical — a retained shop reference, the client's other piece, or a dated photograph taken at the counter — and record the light it was agreed under, since the same finish reads differently under shop lighting, daylight and a phone screen. State what the shop can and cannot control: a plated colour is a property of the deposit chemistry and process the bench runs, so a match is made to a reference within a tolerance judged against that reference, not to a memory or to another maker's finish; a piece with mixed metals or a partly plated assembly will not read uniformly; refreshing one item of a set that the client will wear together makes the untreated items look tired by comparison and that is worth saying out loud. Where an exact match matters more than anything else, the honest options are to treat the whole set, to accept a stated tolerance, or to decline. The agreed reference is retained with the job so the finished piece is judged against the same object at handover.

included: agreeing a physical colour reference and the viewing light
stating the limits of matching across pieces, sets and makers
retaining the reference for the handover comparison
excluded: colour measurement and bath adjustment, which belong to the finish-quality and chemistry specialists
naming a colour standard as a claim
the price difference between colour options

pros.claim: A physical reference agreed under a named light replaces an argument about memory with a comparison anyone can make
pros.example: the client's own second earring kept at the shop as the reference for the one being treated

pros.claim: Saying early that a refreshed piece will outshine its untreated set members prevents a predictable disappointment
pros.example: a client choosing to have all three bangles treated once they picture the mismatch

cons.claim: Retaining a reference piece means holding more of the client's property with all the custody duty that follows
cons.example: the second earring now needing its own tag, storage class and return record

cons.claim: Colour tolerance is a judgement, so a difficult client can dispute a match the bench considers good
cons.example: a client comparing the finished piece under a warm home lamp against the agreed daylight reference

failure_modes: agreeing to match a colour the client describes from memory
not recording the viewing light, so both parties judge the result under different conditions
treating one item of a set without discussing the mismatch that follows
acceptance_tests: every job with a colour expectation records a physical or photographic reference and the light it was agreed under
the retained reference is present and tagged with the job at handover
revisit_triggers: colour disputes recur despite a reference being agreed
the shop changes deposit chemistry or supplier so its achievable colour shifts
shop lighting at the counter changes

base.update_signal: recurring colour disputes, or a chemistry, supplier or lighting change that shifts what the shop can match

nodes.definition: Build the promised date out of the segments that actually consume time and name the ones that are uncertain, rather than quoting the best case and hoping. On a customer piece the segments are the queue ahead of it, the preparation and finishing work itself, any outside step such as a setter unsetting and resetting stones, the process run and any hold the shop imposes before inspection, the inspection itself, and the realistic possibility of one rework cycle. Uncertain segments are stated as uncertain to the client, with the largest single risk usually being an approval gate: a job that needs the client to answer a question cannot move while the phone goes unanswered. The promise given is the date the shop would still keep on a bad week, sentimental deadlines are asked about explicitly because an anniversary or a funeral changes the calculus and sometimes turns into a reason to decline rather than to rush, and any slip is communicated the moment the shop knows rather than on the promised day. Deadlines never buy a shortcut through an approval gate, a safety obligation or an inspection.

included: building the date from named segments including outside steps and one rework cycle
asking about a real deadline and what it implies
communicating a slip as soon as it is known
excluded: trade-account turnaround service levels and reliability as a retention mechanism, owned by the trade-account knowledge base
scheduling and batching economics, owned by the pricing knowledge base
process cycle times at the bench

pros.claim: A date built from named segments makes the promise defensible and the slip explainable
pros.example: telling a client the outside setter is the uncertain segment, so the news that it added days is expected rather than shocking

pros.claim: Asking about the real deadline sometimes converts a rushed job into a declined or deferred one, which is the safer outcome
pros.example: learning a ring is needed for a wedding in three days and offering to book it after the event instead

cons.claim: Padded dates lose work to shops that quote optimistically
cons.example: a client choosing a competitor who promised tomorrow on a job that genuinely needs a week

cons.claim: Naming uncertainty invites the client to negotiate the uncertain segments away
cons.example: a client asking the shop to skip the inspection hold to hit their date

failure_modes: quoting the best case and treating the rework possibility as unlikely
discovering a sentimental deadline only when the client calls upset
letting a promised date pressure a step past an approval gate or an inspection
acceptance_tests: the promised date on each ticket is traceable to named segments including any outside step and one rework allowance
every slip in the record shows the client was informed on the day the shop knew, not on the promised day
revisit_triggers: promised dates are missed often enough to show the segment model is wrong
an outside partner's own turnaround changes
queue volume changes materially

base.update_signal: a pattern of missed dates, or a change in queue volume or an outside partner's turnaround

nodes.definition: Collect one signature on one sheet that carries everything already agreed, and treat that signature as the switch that lets work start rather than as a shield. The sheet references the ticket and its condition photos by number, restates the scope in and out, lists the disclosed risks specific to this piece (the zones that may open, the components excluded from immersion or heat, the unknowns being accepted), carries the wear expectation and the statement that the work is plating rather than solid gold, records the irreplaceability class and the declared value with the shop's plain-language liability position, and names who authorised it and when. The client keeps a copy; the shop retains the signed original with the job file. Two limits are stated on the sheet itself: it does not authorise anything outside the written scope, and it is not a waiver that makes a refused job acceptable, because the refusal criteria sit above any signature. The shop's own counsel and insurer review the wording, and nothing on it is offered as legal advice to the client.

included: the contents of the signed sheet and its reference to the photo set
the rule that the signature starts work and authorises only the written scope
retention of the signed original with the job file
excluded: drafting legal wording, which the shop's counsel does
consumer-rights determinations in the shop's market
per-step approvals during the job, which are a separate gate

pros.claim: One sheet holding scope, risks, wear expectation and class makes the whole agreement checkable in seconds
pros.example: a bench operator confirming before the first irreversible step that the signed sheet covers exactly what is about to happen

pros.claim: Stating on the sheet that it is not a waiver keeps the refusal criteria intact under pressure
pros.example: a client offering to sign anything for a job the criteria decline, and the sheet itself saying that is not how it works

cons.claim: A dense sheet can be signed unread, which weakens its evidential value and its ethical purpose
cons.example: a client signing while their coffee cools, having heard none of the disclosures out loud

cons.claim: Form wording is jurisdiction-specific and must be reviewed and kept current at real cost
cons.example: wording carried over from another market that the shop's own insurer would not accept

failure_modes: starting work on a verbal yes with the sheet to be signed at collection
treating the signature as permission for anything the bench later thinks is needed
a sheet so long the client signs without reading and the disclosures never actually happen
acceptance_tests: no job in the record has bench work logged before its signed sheet, and each sheet references its ticket and photo set
each sheet contains the scope, this piece's specific disclosed risks, the wear expectation, the not-solid-gold statement, the class, the declared value and the liability position
the wording in use is the version reviewed by the shop's counsel and insurer, with the review date recorded
revisit_triggers: a dispute shows the sheet did not cover something it should have
consumer or contract rules in the shop's jurisdiction change
the service menu or the process changes what must be disclosed

base.update_signal: a dispute exposing a gap in the sheet, or a rules or service-menu change that alters what must be disclosed

nodes.definition: Put a named stop in front of every action on a customer piece that cannot be undone, and require a live approval to pass it rather than relying on the signature taken at intake. The gated actions are the ones with no way back: stripping the existing coating, any abrasive finishing that removes metal, unsetting or resetting a stone, applying heat or solder, and any immersion that can attack the substrate, a glued joint or a porous stone. Passing the gate needs four things confirmed in the same minute — the action is inside the written scope, the signed sheet covers this specific risk, nothing discovered since intake has changed the picture, and for irreplaceable pieces the client has approved this step explicitly. The safety and compliance verdict sits above the gate and can close it regardless of client wishes or schedule; a promised date never opens it. Passing is recorded with the time, the action and who approved it, so the job history shows what was authorised before the piece changed forever.

included: the list of gated irreversible actions
the four confirmations required to pass and their recording
the rule that safety and compliance can close the gate and a deadline cannot open it
excluded: how each action is performed at the bench
chemical handling obligations themselves, which the safety specialist owns
quality release of the finished piece

pros.claim: A gate at the last recoverable moment catches the mismatch between what was agreed and what is about to happen
pros.example: a bench operator stopping because the scope excluded the interior the strip would reach

pros.claim: Per-step approval on irreplaceable pieces keeps the client in the decision at the moments that matter
pros.example: phoning before unsetting a stone from a memorial ring even though the sheet already mentions unsetting

cons.claim: Gates fragment bench flow and cost throughput, especially where the client must be reached
cons.example: a batch held because one job needs an approval the client has not answered

cons.claim: Gate discipline decays into a formality if it is never seen to stop anything
cons.example: a checklist ticked in advance for a whole tray so the confirmations happen before the facts do

failure_modes: treating the intake signature as blanket authorisation for every irreversible step
passing the gate on assumption when the client cannot be reached
letting a promised collection date substitute for an approval
acceptance_tests: every irreversible action in the job history has a recorded gate pass with time, action and approver
no gate pass exists for an action outside the written scope, and irreplaceable-class jobs show explicit per-step client approvals
revisit_triggers: an irreversible step is performed without a recorded pass
the process changes so that a new action becomes irreversible
the safety specialist adds an obligation that changes what the gate must confirm

base.update_signal: an irreversible action performed without a recorded pass, or a process change that adds a new unrecoverable step

nodes.definition: Handle the moment the piece turns out not to be what intake thought with a standing procedure rather than improvisation, because that moment is routine in this trade: soft solder appears under the old coating, the substrate beneath a worn plate is not what the marks suggested, a shank shows a crack once the finish is off, a stone moves in its setting, or a hollow form bleeds trapped solution. The procedure is fixed — stop before the next step, secure the piece in its own carrier, photograph the discovery in the state it was found, write what was found and what it changes, and contact the client with three things ready: what this means for the agreed scope, what the honest options now are including returning the piece part-worked, and what each option changes about the timeline and the price mechanism the pricing knowledge base defines. The bench does not decide to press on because the fix seems obvious, and it does not quietly absorb extra work; both hide information the client is entitled to. Where the discovery matches a refusal criterion, the job is stopped and returned even mid-process, which is why the criteria are worth applying hard at intake.

included: the stop, secure, photograph, record and contact sequence
presenting honest options including return part-worked
stopping mid-process when a discovery matches a refusal criterion
excluded: the bench remedy for the discovered condition
re-quoting arithmetic, which the pricing knowledge base owns
structural repair services the shop may not offer

pros.claim: A fixed stop sequence prevents the single worst habit in the trade, which is pressing on to avoid an awkward call
pros.example: a hidden solder seam photographed and reported instead of being heated and hoped through

pros.claim: Photographing the discovery in place preserves the evidence that the condition was pre-existing
pros.example: the crack shown in the strip basket before any further handling, dated against the intake photo of the same zone

cons.claim: Stopping mid-process can leave a piece in a worse cosmetic state than it arrived in while decisions are made
cons.example: a stripped ring sitting unfinished for days because the client cannot be reached

cons.claim: Escalations consume bench and counter time that no quote anticipated
cons.example: two calls, a photo email and a rewritten scope for a job that was priced as routine

failure_modes: continuing because stopping would break the promised date
absorbing the extra work silently and never telling the client what was found
resuming after a phone call without recording what was agreed
acceptance_tests: every mid-job discovery in the record has its discovery photograph, a written description, the client contact and the agreed option recorded before work resumed
no job shows work continuing past a discovery that matched a refusal criterion
revisit_triggers: the same discovery class recurs, indicating an intake survey gap
clients are frequently unreachable at escalation, stranding part-worked pieces
a discovery type appears that the current options set does not cover

base.update_signal: a recurring discovery class that intake should have caught, or repeated stranding of part-worked pieces at escalation

nodes.definition: Close the job in front of the client rather than handing over a bag, because the handover is the last cheap moment to settle anything.
